# Kaleigh Trace

Kaleigh Trace (born 1986) is a Canadian non-fiction writer, sex educator, and disability activist known for her candid and unapologetic exploration of sexuality, queerness, and disability . Her most prominent work, the memoir *Hot, Wet and Shaking: How I Learned to Talk About Sex*, centers her lived experience as a disabled person to challenge societal taboos and normative depictions of sexuality , . Through her writing, public speaking, and therapeutic practice, Trace has become a significant voice in advocating for the desirability, autonomy, and inclusion of disabled bodies within sexual health frameworks , . Her advocacy is imbued with a profound sense of urgency, stemming from a terminal cancer diagnosis she received in October 2022, which has framed her life's work as a testament to "radical aliveness" in the face of mortality , . This dual focus on social critique and personal affirmation defines her impact on contemporary discourse surrounding disability, feminism, and sex positivity.

## Early Life and Formative Experiences

Kaleigh Trace’s identity and subsequent career trajectory are deeply rooted in the formative experiences of her early life, particularly a catastrophic accident that resulted in a permanent physical disability , . Born in 1986, her life took a defining turn at a young age when she sustained severe injuries in a car accident , . The sources provide slightly different ages for the incident, with one indicating she was eight years old and another nine , , . Regardless of the precise year, the timing was crucial, occurring during childhood at a period when bodily awareness, self-perception, and the internalization of societal norms are being established . This accident resulted in a spinal cord injury that led to a visible physical disability, fundamentally shaping her relationship with her own body and her place in the world , .

The physical manifestations of her disability have been consistent across accounts. She grew up ambulating with an unsteady gait, described as swaying, scissoring legs, and experiencing frequent falls . During her childhood, she also used a wheelchair . This physical reality became a source of both hyperawareness and alienation. As she aged, she experienced increasing feelings of estrangement due to the visible differences between her body and the narrow cultural beauty standards prevalent in the mid-2000s, which excluded disabled and queer identities , . These early experiences of navigating a world not built for her body laid the groundwork for her later work as an activist who challenges systemic devaluation of disabled people through inaccessible infrastructure, public staring, and media underrepresentation . Her identity as a disabled person is not viewed as a limitation but as one facet of a complex, multifaceted identity that informs every aspect of her life and work .

Trace identifies as a queer woman, a key component of her intersecting identities , . This aspect of her identity intersects with her disability in her work, where she challenges rigid societal norms around sexuality, gender, and representation , . Her feminist perspective further frames her analysis of power, privilege, and systemic injustice, particularly within sexual health contexts , . This tripartite identity—disabled, queer, and feminist—is foundational to her worldview and the lens through which she engages with the world as a writer and educator , . Growing up, she had to learn her body and how to be sexual within it in a way that was different from most people, a journey she chronicles extensively in her memoir . This process of self-discovery, forged in the crucible of her unique experiences, became the raw material for her groundbreaking advocacy and writing.

Her educational background reflects a path toward understanding human relationships and well-being. She graduated from Dalhousie University in Halifax with a Bachelor of Arts in 2009 . Later, she pursued advanced studies in therapy, beginning a Master of Science program in Couples and Family Therapy at the University of Guelph in 2017 while commuting from Toronto . This academic pursuit represents a significant evolution in her career, moving from direct public education and activism into clinical practice. As a student, she already identified as a Registered Psychotherapist with the College of Registered Psychotherapists of Ontario, framing her therapeutic work as "justice-doing," where she integrates a critical analysis of systems of power and privilege into her sessions . This formal training provides a structured methodology to complement the experiential knowledge she gained through her earlier work, allowing her to contribute to healing shame and creating inclusive spaces in a professional therapeutic context . Her educational journey underscores her commitment to both theoretical understanding and practical application in her mission to foster healthier, more equitable conversations about sex and identity.

## Career and Major Works

Kaleigh Trace’s career is anchored by her debut memoir, *Hot, Wet and Shaking: How I Learned to Talk About Sex*, a work that has become the cornerstone of her public identity and a significant contribution to contemporary non-fiction literature , . The book originated from a personal blog she wrote called 'The Fucking Facts', which documented her experiences with sexual pleasure as a disabled woman , , . This blog served as the foundation upon which the memoir was built, capturing her journey toward embracing her identity as both queer and disabled . The book was first published in 2014 by Invisible Publishing , . Its release was met with immediate attention and positive reception, with one reviewer noting having heard many good things about it prior to purchasing it at the Toronto International Book Fair in November 2014 . The memoir explores her path to sexual self-understanding through a series of candid, humorous, and vulnerable personal narratives that spare no details , . It is described as accessible, authentic, and free of theoretical abstraction, instead offering intimate stories that feel like confiding in a best friend . This relatable tone lowers barriers for readers confronting difficult and taboo subjects.

The content of *Hot, Wet and Shaking* directly confronts and dismantles normative, able-bodied, homogeneous depictions of sexuality . The book delves into a wide range of topics that are often considered unspeakable, including bladder accessibility challenges, potty humor in intimate contexts, explorations of sex toys, positions, and masturbation . It also addresses struggles with orgasm, bodily autonomy, and street harassment . A particularly poignant chapter, titled 'Looking for Blood,' details her abortion experience and highlights the barriers to reproductive choice faced by women in Nova Scotia . The narrative is rich with specific anecdotes, such as early experiments with sex education using a banana and plum, accidentally retrieving a sex toy in a supermarket, and being caught masturbating while driving . By centering her own lived experience, Trace rejects the dominant literary approach that seeks to define or deconstruct disability and instead presents it as an inherent, untheorized part of her personal story . This approach affirms diversity, authenticity, and unashamed self-definition . The book won the Evelyn Richardson Non-Fiction Award, cementing its critical acclaim .

The enduring relevance of her work is demonstrated by its continued publication and engagement. In June 2024, the book was republished in a 10th-anniversary edition by Invisible Publishing , . This new edition included additional essays and a foreword by author Christa Couture, signaling the book's lasting influence and its continued importance in the conversation around disability and sexuality . The act of editing this anniversary edition while planning for her death was described by Trace as an "editorial conversation with her younger self," conducted amid a prognosis of two years to live . This context adds a profound layer of meaning to the memoir, reframing it not just as a piece of social commentary but as a conscious practice of radical aliveness . The book's back cover describes its contents as discussions of "her sexual exploits, bodily negotiations and attempts at adulthood, sparing none of the details and assuming you are not polite company," a fitting summary of its bold and unflinching nature . The success of the book and its anniversary edition confirms its resonance with audiences seeking more inclusive and honest narratives about sex and disability .

Beyond her memoir, Trace maintains an active online presence through her website, kaleightrace.com, which succeeded her original blog, thefuckingfacts.com . While the provided sources do not detail recent writings beyond her blog posts and the memoir, her continued existence as a writer and sex educator suggests an ongoing engagement with these themes . Her work ethic emphasizes listening, kindness, and empathy, principles she applies in all her communication about sex . This commitment to fostering comfortable and honest dialogue is a hallmark of her entire career, from her earliest blog posts to her later therapeutic practice , . The progression from a personal blog to a critically acclaimed, award-winning memoir illustrates a clear and impactful trajectory, establishing her as a pioneering author whose work has reshaped the landscape of sex-positive and disability-inclusive literature.

## Professional Roles and Activism

Kaleigh Trace’s professional life is a tapestry woven from multiple roles that collectively advance her mission to dismantle societal taboos and create inclusive spaces for marginalized voices. Her work as a sex educator, therapist, and public advocate is consistently informed by her identity as a disabled queer woman and her feminist politics , . One of the most formative and frequently cited aspects of her career was her five-year tenure working at Venus Envy, a queer, feminist, and education-based sex-and-book shop in Halifax, Nova Scotia , , . She began working there at the age of 23 after graduating from university . This experience was transformative for her, described as "revolutionary" for the way it reshaped her understanding of human desirability and value . At Venus Envy, she ran workshops on various sex-related topics and focused on dismantling misinformation, fostering honest dialogue, and providing a space where people could ask questions without shame , . This hands-on work in a community-facing sex shop provided her with invaluable experience in direct education and allowed her to see firsthand the diverse ways people engage with their sexuality, which later informed her writing and public speaking .

Following her time in direct education, Trace pursued a Master of Science in Couple & Family Therapy from the University of Guelph, commencing her studies in 2017 . This academic path marks a significant shift towards clinical practice, positioning her to apply her lived experience and passion for justice within a therapeutic framework. As a registered psychotherapist, she integrates a critical analysis of systems of power and privilege into her work, framing therapy itself as "justice-doing work" . This approach allows her to address individual and relational issues while simultaneously challenging the broader social structures that create harm and limit access to well-being for marginalized communities, including disabled individuals . Her therapeutic practice is therefore an extension of her activism, applying her skills to help heal shame and create more inclusive and equitable relationships at an interpersonal level . Her work at Venus Envy, spanning a decade before becoming a therapist, shows a deep and sustained commitment to sexual health education, demonstrating a clear progression from public-facing outreach to private therapeutic intervention .

As an activist, Trace’s work is centered on challenging harmful misconceptions about disability and sex. She explicitly names the biggest misconception as the assumption that disabled people lack sexual desire or partners because they are perceived as undesirable . By openly discussing her own sexuality, desires, and experiences, she actively refutes this pervasive stereotype . Her activism is inherently intersectional, addressing the interconnectedness of disability, queerness, race, fatness, age, and representation . For example, in her writing, she discusses the intersection of femme presentation with dyke identity, exploring the nuances of gendered appearance norms . She also advocates for the valuation of disabled bodies within sexual health frameworks, arguing against the systemic devaluation of disabled people that manifests in inaccessible infrastructure and media underrepresentation . Her collaboration with fellow disability activist Andrew Gurza on his podcast, 'Disability After Dark', to discuss inclusive sex education and consent exemplifies her commitment to public dialogue on these crucial issues . Trace believes that people don't know how to understand disabled bodies as desirable, and her work is a direct attempt to change that fundamental lack of understanding .

Trace draws inspiration from a community of disabled activists and writers whom she cites as role models. These include Loree Erikson, Andrew Gurza, Eli Clare, Lyric Seal, Mia Mingus, and Mia Gimp . Engaging with their work situates her own within a larger tradition of disability justice and queer liberation. Her activism is not limited to writing; it extends to her public presence as a speaker and performer. She has participated in literary events, given readings, and engaged in book tours, using these platforms to share her work and connect with audiences directly , . Her participation in these events, often alongside other LGBTQ+ authors and artists, reinforces her standing within the literary and activist communities . Through these varied professional roles and forms of activism, Trace builds a multi-pronged approach to social change, combining public education, clinical practice, creative expression, and direct community engagement to challenge ableism and promote a more inclusive vision of human sexuality.

## Public Engagement and Literary Presence

Kaleigh Trace has cultivated a robust public presence through a combination of literary events, media appearances, and community engagement, ensuring her message reaches a wide and diverse audience. Her work as a writer and speaker has been featured in numerous public forums, solidifying her reputation as a leading voice on disability, sexuality, and queerness. In July 2025, she participated in the Universal Dawn literary event hosted by Halifax poet Andrew Patterson during SappyFest 10 in Sackville, New Brunswick . This event, which took place over the New Brunswick Day long weekend (July 18–20), was a curated component of a major festival, confirming her standing within the regional literary scene . Her appearance alongside other authors and artists at this festival demonstrates her integration into the broader arts community . During the event, she read excerpts from her work, addressing themes of disability, queer identity, abortion, and gendered appearance norms, connecting directly with attendees through her performance .

In addition to literary festivals, Trace has undertaken book tours to promote her work and engage with readers. Following the release of her memoir, she embarked on a tour that included stops at the University of King’s College in Halifax, the University of Guelph, and a reading in Sackville organized by the reformed Women’s and Gender Studies Society . She also held a public reading event in Ottawa at the location of Venus Envy, highlighting the connection between her book and the shop where she once worked . These tours demonstrate a deliberate effort to build community and facilitate dialogue around the sensitive and important topics she explores in her writing. Her participation in such events is not merely promotional; it is a continuation of her activist work, providing a platform for open and honest conversation that challenges societal discomfort with disability and sexuality .

Her public presence extends to digital and media platforms. An interview mentioned in one source, though the specific outlet is not named, detailed her views on sex and disability, emphasizing her belief that "People don't know how to understand disabled bodies as desirable" . This interview showcases her willingness to engage with media to broaden the reach of her message. Furthermore, her collaboration with Andrew Gurza on his podcast, 'Disability After Dark', is a significant public engagement activity . This platform allows her to discuss complex issues like inclusive sex education, consent, and the need to value disabled bodies within sexual health frameworks in a format that can reach a global audience . Such collaborations position her as a thought leader within the disability rights movement, sharing her expertise and perspectives with a wider listenership.

Trace’s work has also garnered attention within academic and literary circles. She is listed in the 'List of LGBTQ writers', categorized as a Canadian non-fiction writer whose notable work is *Hot, Wet, and Shaking: How I Learned to Talk About Sex* . This inclusion signifies her recognition as a significant contributor to LGBTQ literature. The critical praise for her book, such as the description of it as a "groundbreaking contribution" that centers disability as an inherent part of personal narrative, indicates its respected place in contemporary non-fiction . The fact that it was selected for feature on the 49th Shelf main page and recommended by word-of-mouth at a major book fair shortly after its release points to its immediate impact and resonant quality among readers and reviewers . Her continued public engagement through readings, tours, and interviews ensures that her literary presence remains vibrant and her ideas continue to circulate within both activist and mainstream cultural spheres.

## Personal Life and Terminal Illness

Kaleigh Trace’s personal life is intrinsically linked to her public work, as her identity as a queer, disabled woman serves as the foundation for her advocacy and writing. She resides in Toronto but splits her time with Nova Scotia, maintaining a connection to the city where she worked at Venus Envy and began her career . This geographic duality reflects a balance between her professional life as a couples and family therapist and her roots in the community that shaped her early activism. Her identity is consistently defined by the intersection of her queer, disabled, and feminist selves, a framework she uses to analyze the world and communicate her message , , . This multifaceted identity is not a collection of separate traits but a cohesive whole that informs her perspective on everything from sex and relationships to social justice and healthcare.

A profoundly significant and defining aspect of her life, which adds a layer of urgency and poignancy to her entire body of work, is her health status. In early 2024, she was diagnosed with terminal cancer and was given a prognosis of two years to live . The exact details of her diagnosis, such as the type or stage of cancer, are not provided in the available sources, which is appropriate for an encyclopedic entry focusing on her public persona and contributions rather than private medical information . However, the diagnosis itself is a central biographical fact that shapes the interpretation of her legacy. It is the context for her final major project: the 10th-anniversary re-publication of her memoir, *Hot, Wet and Shaking* . She described editing this new edition as an "editorial conversation with her younger self," a task she undertook while consciously planning for her death .

This framing transforms her life's work from a simple advocacy project into a powerful testament to "radical aliveness." The phrase, cited from psychoanalyst D.W. Winnicott—"Oh God! May I be alive when I die!"—captures the spirit of her actions . Rather than retreating from public life, she chose to amplify her voice and refine her message in the face of her mortality. Her writing and activism become acts of defiance against the stereotypes and assumptions she spends her life fighting. She is not portrayed as a passive object of pity or a cautionary tale; instead, she is an active agent creating meaning, building community, and leaving a lasting legacy. Her decision to publish a new edition of her memoir, a book that so intimately documents her body, desires, and vulnerabilities, becomes a profound statement about living fully and authentically until the very end. This context connects her personal journey to universal questions of mortality, purpose, and the human desire to be seen, valued, and remembered. Her work thus gains a deeper philosophical dimension, serving as an urgent call to embrace life and love in all its messy, imperfect, and beautiful complexity, especially in the face of its inevitable conclusion.

## Legacy and Critical Reception

Kaleigh Trace’s legacy is that of a pioneering voice who has fundamentally altered the discourse around disability and sexuality in Canada and beyond. Her work is characterized by its radical honesty, its refusal to shy away from taboo subjects, and its unwavering commitment to centering the lived experience of a disabled person. Critics and readers have responded to her writing with significant acclaim, recognizing its groundbreaking nature. The memoir *Hot, Wet and Shaking* is widely praised for its innovative approach, which contrasts sharply with dominant academic or literary traditions that often seek to define, deconstruct, or theorize disability as a subject separate from the personal narrative . Instead, Trace presents disability as an inherent, untheorized part of her story, a method lauded for its intimacy and accessibility . The book's narrative style, described as candid, humorous, and vulnerable, has been credited with making difficult topics approachable and relatable, likened to confiding in a best friend , .

Her critical reception has been overwhelmingly positive, reflecting the resonance of her message. The memoir won the prestigious Evelyn Richardson Non-Fiction Award, a clear indicator of its literary merit and impact within the Canadian publishing industry . Reviews have highlighted its importance in affirming diversity, authenticity, and unashamed self-definition, rejecting normative depictions of sexuality and celebrating the complexities of her identity . The enduring popularity of the book, evidenced by its purchase at a major book fair shortly after its release and its subsequent 10th-anniversary re-publication, attests to its lasting relevance and influence , . The re-publication, which included a new foreword by Christa Couture, further solidified its place as a canonical text in disability and LGBTQ literature . Trace is recognized as a significant figure in the 'List of LGBTQ writers', a testament to her impact on queer literature and culture .

Ultimately, Kaleigh Trace’s legacy is twofold. First, she has made an indelible mark on literature and activism by creating a space where disabled, queer, and feminist voices can speak with authority and vulnerability about sex and desire. She has challenged the pervasive myth that disabled people are asexual, thereby contributing to a more inclusive and accurate understanding of human sexuality , . Second, her legacy is profoundly shaped by her confrontation with mortality. Her terminal illness has transformed her work into a powerful testament to "radical aliveness," a conscious practice of being present and vibrant in the face of an imminent end . This context gives her message a unique urgency and emotional depth. She leaves behind not only a body of influential writing but also an example of living authentically and defiantly until the last possible moment. Her life and work serve as a reminder of the power of storytelling to challenge stigma, inspire change, and find profound meaning in the face of mortality.

These role models include Loree Erikson, Andrew Gurza, Eli Clare, Lyric Seal, Mia Mingus, and Mia Gimp.
Engaging with their work situates Kaleigh Trace's own within a larger tradition of disability justice and queer liberation.
Kaleigh Trace's activism is not limited to writing; it extends to her public presence as a speaker and performer.
Kaleigh Trace has participated in literary events, given readings, and engaged in book tours, using these platforms to share her work and connect with audiences directly.
Kaleigh Trace's participation in these events, often alongside other LGBTQ+ authors and artists, reinforces her standing within the literary and activist communities.

Through these varied professional roles and forms of activism, Kaleigh Trace builds a multi-pronged approach to social change, combining public education, clinical practice, creative expression, and direct community engagement to challenge ableism and promote a more inclusive vision of human sexuality.
Kaleigh Trace has cultivated a robust public presence through a combination of literary events, media appearances, and community engagement, ensuring her message reaches a wide and diverse audience.
Kaleigh Trace's work as a writer and speaker has been featured in numerous public forums, solidifying her reputation as a leading voice on disability, sexuality, and queerness.
In July 2025, Kaleigh Trace participated in the Universal Dawn literary event hosted by Halifax poet Andrew Patterson during SappyFest 10 in Sackville, New Brunswick.
This event, which took place over the New Brunswick Day long weekend (July 18–20), was a curated component of a major festival, confirming Kaleigh Trace's standing within the regional literary scene.
Kaleigh Trace's appearance alongside other authors and artists at this festival demonstrates her integration into the broader arts community.

During the event, Kaleigh Trace read excerpts from her work, addressing themes of disability, queer identity, abortion, and gendered appearance norms, connecting directly with attendees through her performance.
In addition to literary festivals, Kaleigh Trace has undertaken book tours to promote her work and engage with readers.

Following the release of her memoir, Kaleigh Trace embarked on a tour that included stops at the University of King’s College in Halifax, the University of Guelph, and a reading in Sackville organized by the reformed Women’s and Gender Studies Society.
Kaleigh Trace also held a public reading event in Ottawa at the location of Venus Envy, highlighting the connection between her book and the shop where she once worked.
These tours demonstrate a deliberate effort by Kaleigh Trace to build community and facilitate dialogue around the sensitive and important topics she explores in her writing.

Kaleigh Trace's participation in such events is not merely promotional; it is a continuation of her activist work, providing a platform for open and honest conversation that challenges societal discomfort with disability and sexuality.
Kaleigh Trace's public presence extends to digital and media platforms.

An interview mentioned in one source, though the specific outlet is not named, detailed Kaleigh Trace's views on sex and disability, emphasizing her belief that "People don't know how to understand disabled bodies as desirable."
This interview showcases Kaleigh Trace's willingness to engage with media to broaden the reach of her message.
Furthermore, Kaleigh Trace's collaboration with Andrew Gurza on his podcast, 'Disability After Dark', is a significant public engagement activity.

This platform allows Kaleigh Trace to discuss complex issues like inclusive sex education, consent, and the need to value disabled bodies within sexual health frameworks in a format that can reach a global audience.
Such collaborations position Kaleigh Trace as a thought leader within the disability rights movement, sharing her expertise and perspectives with a wider listenership.
Trace’s work has also garnered attention within academic and literary circles.
Kaleigh Trace is listed in the 'List of LGBTQ writers', categorized as a Canadian non-fiction writer whose notable work is *Hot, Wet, and Shaking: How I Learned to Talk About Sex*.
This inclusion signifies Kaleigh Trace's recognition as a significant contributor to LGBTQ literature.

The critical praise for Kaleigh Trace's book, such as the description of it as a "groundbreaking contribution" that centers disability as an inherent part of personal narrative, indicates its respected place in contemporary non-fiction.

The fact that *Hot, Wet and Shaking* was selected for feature on the 49th Shelf main page and recommended by word-of-mouth at a major book fair shortly after its release points to its immediate impact and resonant quality among readers and reviewers.

Kaleigh Trace's continued public engagement through readings, tours, and interviews ensures that her literary presence remains vibrant and her ideas continue to circulate within both activist and mainstream cultural spheres.
Kaleigh Trace’s personal life is intrinsically linked to her public work, as her identity as a queer, disabled woman serves as the foundation for her advocacy and writing.
Kaleigh Trace resides in Toronto but splits her time with Nova Scotia, maintaining a connection to the city where she worked at Venus Envy and began her career.
This geographic duality reflects a balance between Kaleigh Trace's professional life as a couples and family therapist and her roots in the community that shaped her early activism.
Kaleigh Trace's identity is consistently defined by the intersection of her queer, disabled, and feminist selves, a framework she uses to analyze the world and communicate her message.

This multifaceted identity is not a collection of separate traits but a cohesive whole that informs Kaleigh Trace's perspective on everything from sex and relationships to social justice and healthcare.
A profoundly significant and defining aspect of Kaleigh Trace's life, which adds a layer of urgency and poignancy to her entire body of work, is her health status.
In early 2024, Kaleigh Trace was diagnosed with terminal cancer and was given a prognosis of two years to live.

The exact details of Kaleigh Trace's diagnosis, such as the type or stage of cancer, are not provided in the available sources, which is appropriate for an encyclopedic entry focusing on her public persona and contributions rather than private medical information.
However, the diagnosis itself is a central biographical fact that shapes the interpretation of Kaleigh Trace's legacy.
It is the context for Kaleigh Trace's final major project: the 10th-anniversary re-publication of her memoir, *Hot, Wet and Shaking*.
Kaleigh Trace described editing this new edition as an "editorial conversation with her younger self," a task she undertook while consciously planning for her death.
This framing transforms Kaleigh Trace's life's work from a simple advocacy project into a powerful testament to "radical aliveness."
The phrase "Oh God! May I be alive when I die!" cited from psychoanalyst D.W. Winnicott, captures the spirit of Kaleigh Trace's actions.
Rather than retreating from public life, Kaleigh Trace chose to amplify her voice and refine her message in the face of her mortality.
Kaleigh Trace's writing and activism become acts of defiance against the stereotypes and assumptions she spends her life fighting.
Kaleigh Trace is not portrayed as a passive object of pity or a cautionary tale; instead, she is an active agent creating meaning, building community, and leaving a lasting legacy.

Kaleigh Trace's decision to publish a new edition of her memoir, a book that so intimately documents her body, desires, and vulnerabilities, becomes a profound statement about living fully and authentically until the very end.
This context connects Kaleigh Trace's personal journey to universal questions of mortality, purpose, and the human desire to be seen, valued, and remembered.

Kaleigh Trace's work thus gains a deeper philosophical dimension, serving as an urgent call to embrace life and love in all its messy, imperfect, and beautiful complexity, especially in the face of its inevitable conclusion.
Kaleigh Trace’s legacy is that of a pioneering voice who has fundamentally altered the discourse around disability and sexuality in Canada and beyond.
Kaleigh Trace's work is characterized by its radical honesty, its refusal to shy away from taboo subjects, and its unwavering commitment to centering the lived experience of a disabled person.
Critics and readers have responded to Kaleigh Trace's writing with significant acclaim, recognizing its groundbreaking nature.

The memoir *Hot, Wet and Shaking* is widely praised for its innovative approach, which contrasts sharply with dominant academic or literary traditions that often seek to define, deconstruct, or theorize disability as a subject separate from the personal narrative.
Instead, Kaleigh Trace presents disability as an inherent, untheorized part of her story, a method lauded for its intimacy and accessibility.
The book's narrative style, described as candid, humorous, and vulnerable, has been credited with making difficult topics approachable and relatable, likened to confiding in a best friend.
Kaleigh Trace's critical reception has been overwhelmingly positive, reflecting the resonance of her message.
The memoir *Hot, Wet and Shaking* won the prestigious Evelyn Richardson Non-Fiction Award, a clear indicator of its literary merit and impact within the Canadian publishing industry.

Reviews have highlighted the importance of *Hot, Wet and Shaking* in affirming diversity, authenticity, and unashamed self-definition, rejecting normative depictions of sexuality and celebrating the complexities of Kaleigh Trace's identity.

The enduring popularity of the book *Hot, Wet and Shaking*, evidenced by its purchase at a major book fair shortly after its release and its subsequent 10th-anniversary re-publication, attests to its lasting relevance and influence.
The re-publication of *Hot, Wet and Shaking*, which included a new foreword by Christa Couture, further solidified its place as a canonical text in disability and LGBTQ literature.
Kaleigh Trace is recognized as a significant figure in the 'List of LGBTQ writers', a testament to her impact on queer literature and culture.
Ultimately, Kaleigh Trace’s legacy is twofold.

First, Kaleigh Trace has made an indelible mark on literature and activism by creating a space where disabled, queer, and feminist voices can speak with authority and vulnerability about sex and desire.
Kaleigh Trace has challenged the pervasive myth that disabled people are asexual, thereby contributing to a more inclusive and accurate understanding of human sexuality.
Second, Kaleigh Trace's legacy is profoundly shaped by her confrontation with mortality.
Kaleigh Trace's terminal illness has transformed her work into a powerful testament to "radical aliveness," a conscious practice of being present and vibrant in the face of an imminent end.
This context gives Kaleigh Trace's message a unique urgency and emotional depth.
Kaleigh Trace leaves behind not only a body of influential writing but also an example of living authentically and defiantly until the last possible moment.
Kaleigh Trace's life and work serve as a reminder of the power of storytelling to challenge stigma, inspire change, and find profound meaning in the face of mortality.

[The Current](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/thecurrent/the-current-for-october-30-2017-1.4375925)

For young people with cognitive and physical disabilities "sex ed" is virtually non-existent. Disability activists are fighting to change that, to make sure their needs are included too.

'People don't know how to understand disabled bodies as desirable,' says Kaleigh Trace
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 1](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.4375960,1552063689000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C122%2C5793%2C3258%29%3B)

Andrew Gurza has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair. He says the world sees people with disabilities as asexual and as a result is excluded from proper sex education. (Paul Jamnicky, 2017)

_Originally published Oct 30, 2017._

[Read Story Transcript](http://www.cbc.ca/radio/thecurrent/the-current-for-october-30-2017-1.4375925/monday-october-30-2017-full-episode-transcript-1.4379150#segment2)

When [Andrew Gurza](http://www.andrewgurza.com/) went to the hospital for an STI (sexually transmitted infection) test last year, he says the nurse was surprised he needed one.

"She looked me up and down and said, 'Oh! Why are you here for that?'" the 33-year-old Toronto man tells _The Current'_s Anna Maria Tremonti.

![Image 2](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.4375964,1509362655000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C448%2C512%29%3B)

Andrew Gurza says people would rather just avoid the topic of disability and sex because for many, it's too much to handle. (Alice Xue, 2017)

"I kind of just said 'because I'm sexually active.'"

Gurza says this experience at the hospital is not uncommon when he talks about sex.

"I have sex. Get over it, " says Gurza who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair.

He's one of many people with disabilities who are calling for better sex information at school and at the doctor's office.

Even Canada's own sex-ed guide says there's often a lack of good material for people whose bodies and minds aren't typical. In Gurza's case, he says he giggled through a sex-ed curriculum that included nothing about what his own sexual experiences would be like.

He wants people to get past the taboo of talking about sex and disability so the disabled experience is reflected in the current sex-ed curriculum — in a way that "values the disabled body."

Now more than two decades later,  Gurza's podcast, [Disability After Dark](http://www.andrewgurza.com/disability-after-dark/) is devoted entirely to the topic. One of the issues he's covered is how to talk about sex with a new care attendant, an awkward conversation he's personally had to face because he sometimes needs an attendant to help him prepare for sex.

"Bodies don't all work the same," says disability activist [Kaleigh Trace](http://www.kaleightrace.com/), who joined Gurza on the show.

"People don't know how to understand disabled bodies as desirable."

![Image 3](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.4375966,1509363831000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C380%2C6016%2C3462%29%3B)

Kaleigh Trace is a sex educator who has a spinal cord injury. She tours high schools and universities speaking about sex and disabilities.

For 24-year-old Jessica Coole of New Minas, N.S., sex ed in middle school was traumatizing.

"I'm like how do they do all this?" says Coole who has a cognitive disability. The information she was given in class left her so confused that years later, after fooling around with her boyfriend but not having sex, she was concerned she got pregnant.

Jessica's mother, Michelle Morgan-Coole, says she struggled to get sex information her daughter could understand. The topic remains a tough one for them today.

"I do want to protect her," says Morgan-Coole.

![Image 4](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.4375971,1509372731000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%28113%2C0%2C3019%2C2448%29%3B)

For Jessica Coole and her mother Michelle Morgan-Coole in New Minas, N.S., sex is a difficult topic. 'I do want to protect her,' says Morgan-Coole. (Michelle Morgan-Coole)

"It's not easy and it's not fun. It's hard to talk about."

Shaniff Esmail has helped many people make the conversation easier. Earlier this year, through his work as a professor and the associate chair in rehabilitation at the University of Alberta, he helped develop an online program for health-care workers on how to respectfully talk about sex with disabled patients.

Doctors are often relieved when disabled patients don't bring up sex because the topic's still taboo, Esmail says. He suggests one of the main reasons for that is the issue of consent, which can be complicated for people who have cognitive impairments.

"A lot of times these individuals have the capacity but they are not offered the choice," he explains, pointing to how doctors often fail to offer birth control to patients with cognitive disabilities.

Esmail has also helped parents not only get their children good sex information, he's guided them on how to support healthy sex lives.

He tells Tremonti, how he once helped a cognitively-challenged teenager who had been acting sexually aggressive at school by putting him on a schedule where he was encouraged to masturbate before and after school.

"In terms of his inappropriate sexual behaviours, they stopped once we started him on this schedule," says Esmail.

"It was amazing the difference in his behaviours."

**Listen to the full conversation above.**

_This segment was produced by Halfiax network producer Mary-Catherine McIntosh._

For all of the talking our culture does about sex, it seems we’re not really saying that much. We’re a society saturated with dirty talk, yet so much of it is sanctioned by the status quo, its depictions homogeneous and its players near identical. In all the tell-alls, how-tos, and titillations we’re missing real diversity, along with authentic voices to tell the truth about sex in all its messy, euphoric, complicated and often hilarious glory. When a writer comes along who is willing to delve into those truths via her own life experience, it’s hard not to be immediately grateful.

Twenty-eight-year-old Kaleigh Trace is a self-described disabled, queer, feminist sex educator, who, from her home base in Halifax, works at the award-winning sex shop Venus Envy. Her memoir, _Hot, Wet, and Shaking_, is a natural extension of her candid sex writing career — from the novice erotica she wrote after not seeing people like herself in depictions of sexuality (“Everything I had read, watched and done had been about being able-bodied, something I was just not and did not want to be,”) to her popular sexual education blog, The F–king Facts. Her memoir lays out the path that brought her to these definitions and vocations, and is always frank about the bumps and humiliations along the way.

“I would prefer to be honest,” Trace asserts. “May all my inexpert errors reassure you: You are not alone.”

As a child, Trace suffered a severe spinal cord injury in a car accident, causing her to spend part of her childhood in a wheelchair. “Today, I amble around with a serious swagger. It looks a little like I’m always dancing.” Though disability is a large part of how Trace relates to both her body and the world, it is, of course, only part of who she is, and in the introduction she is quick to assert an identity beyond it. Though this book certainly is about how Trace’s disability has forced her to approach sexuality differently, it is accessible to anyone who has struggled and faced confusion on the path to pleasure — so basically, everyone. In fact, the very idea of “differently” presupposes that there is a standard way, something that Trace adamantly refutes. “Identities are complex and incongruous, multi-faceted and impossible to circumnavigate,” she writes.

_Hot, Wet, and Shaking_ is written in the tone of a trusted and cheeky friend, confessing secrets that shake loose their shame when spoken aloud. This is not the sex advice of a poised, multi-orgasmic, inaccessible, or clinical expert, but rather the honest musings of a woman in a pair of yesterday’s dirty jeans. Trace describes how it was a love of feminist literature that got her into Venus Envy, and how working there expanded her thoughts and views on sex and its participants. Her depiction of herself as a messy, comedic heroine, an unlikely and even unqualified sex educator, adds weight to the value of her advice, as we come to immediately trust her as she hilariously catalogues her flaws and foibles for all to see.

Trace tells comical tales of early sex instruction involving a banana and a plum, of accidentally urinating in bed with a gratefully understanding partner, of her own fumbling struggle to orgasm and the various implements that got her there. While driving, she gets busted with her hand down her pants by a surprised truck driver. While at the supermarket, she accidentally pulls out a sex toy from her bag to the alarm of other patrons. She wonders if a particularly visceral attraction to someone is actually the stomach flu. We fall in love with her not only because we see ourselves in the stories she tells, but because of how readily and refreshingly she forgives herself for her failings and moves forward.

This advertisement has not loaded yet.

This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below.

Though the book is predominately fun and funny, it does take moments to navigate into more serious territory. A chapter devoted to Trace’s abortion, titled “Looking for Blood,” is particularly moving both in its honesty and its articulation of barriers to choice for women in Nova Scotia. A chapter that touches on both ableism and street harassment drives home that no matter how confident and self-assured you will yourself to be, the world often answers by trying to push you down again.

During it all, Trace is defiant. “\[I\] swallowed that shame down and left it to rot in my guts,” she writes. “F–k it. Everyone can kiss my ass, I decided. I have always looked different. I will always be different. This will never change, and even though there are times when it is difficult, I have made it my own personal project to never be ashamed of myself.”

When Trace is unashamed, her reader is unashamed along with her. Most will see themselves in some facet of her story, all of us influenced by a dominant narrative of what sex should be and has to look like, and who is allowed to enjoy it. What actually makes Trace’s memoir so compelling is the undercurrent of her own fear and doubt — she asks her reader to be gentle with her, she questions the quality of her own writing, she even doubts her authority to speak on the subject. You can tell it took a great deal for her to tell her story, but that she sees a higher purpose to her book — and to all her work — that belies her own insecurities. In short, Trace wants, above all else, to help people.

“I wrote a book for reasons I feel are worth it,” she writes. “I did not expose my sex life, my inner monologue, and all of my not-so-secret-secrets for nothing.” It is this sincerity that separates _Hot, Wet, and Shaking_ from mere salacious or instructional document. Trace is telling us about her parts, her exploits, her failures, and her pleasures in order to bring comfort to the lonely — to assure those who wonder where exactly they fit in that there is a place for them. That she found it, and they can too.

Kaleigh Trace explores sex through lens of disabled person
==========================================================

Hot, Wet and Shaking launches Sept 17 at Venus Envy

By [Jeremy Willard](https://xtramagazine.com/contributor/jeremy-willard) • September 12, 2014 4:00 am EDT

![Image 1](https://xtramagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/XO270-OITC1.jpg)

Kaleigh Trace writes about navigating sexual situations as a queer, disabled woman in her book Hot, Wet and Shaking. Credit: Krista Comeau

From performance anxiety to difficulty achieving orgasm, everyone experiences sex-related complications of some kind, but it’s difficult for most able-bodied people to imagine what sex might be like for somebody with a disability. Depending on the particular disability, activities that most able-bodied people take for granted may have to be approached in a very different way.

Kaleigh Trace is a disabled queer woman, and in her new book, _Hot, Wet and Shaking: How I Learned to Talk About Sex_, she relates her experiences navigating sexual situations. While not all of her book directly addresses sex and disability, her various serious, amusing and often sexy anecdotes look at sex through the lens of someone with a disability.

Advertisement

“I was in a car accident when I was nine and sustained some pretty catastrophic injuries. Now I’m 28, so for most of my life and all of my adult life I’ve been disabled,” Trace says. “I’ve had to learn my body and how to be sexual in this body in a different way from most people.”

Candour is required for a book of this sort to be hard-hitting, and Trace seems to have a boatload of it.

“I have a lot of bladder stuff. I can’t hold my pee very long, so part of being out in public for me is navigating bathrooms. Where can I find them? Are they accessible? So there’s a lot of potty humour in the book,” Trace says. “Like what happens when I have to pee when hooking up with somebody for the first time.”

[Subscribe Now](https://subscribe.xtramagazine.com/)

Trace is a sex educator at Venus Envy in Halifax, running workshops on sex and sex-related topics. She also maintains a sex advice blog called Fucking Facts. So, sex is kind of her thing, but this is her first time writing something focused mostly on her personal experiences.

At the Ottawa launch of her book, Trace will not only read passages from her work, but will talk about sex and disability in general, including such topics as sex toys, positions and masturbation.

“I feel pretty happy about a lot of parts of my life, and this book is about the things in my life that I love and about the stuff I’m still trying to figure out. I’m still working on understanding what being disabled can look like for me,” Trace says.

![Image 1: "I wrote a book about learning to love my body. After finding out I have terminal cancer, I’ve decided to republish it"](https://torontolife.mblycdn.com/tl/resized/2024/08/w1280/KT-arms-raised.jpg)

I grew up feeling inherently undesirable. When I was eight years old, I was in a car accident where I sustained a spinal cord injury. It left me permanently disabled. Whether I wanted to or not, I always drew attention to myself. I swayed when I walked, my legs scissored in and out, and I often tumbled over completely. It was the mid-2000s, and celebrities like Britney Spears and Christina Aguilera were the pinnacle of beauty and sex appeal, but they were thin and able bodied. I couldn’t see myself in them.

[_**Related:** “I dropped out of high school due to ADHD and depression. Public libraries saved my life—and now I’m getting a master’s degree”_](https://torontolife.com/memoir/nancy-dutra-high-school-drop-out-libraries-self-taught/)

Then, in 2009, I graduated from Dalhousie University with a bachelor of arts—not a super useful degree in the middle of a global recession. I desperately needed a job, and Venus Envy, an education-based sex-and-book shop, was one of the best bookstores in Halifax. I really wanted to work there because the store had an incredible collection of feminist critical theory. Admittedly, I was less interested in the sex toys. At 23 years old, I was mostly indifferent to sex. I was inexperienced, and though I was queer, I’d been in the closet for years. But I had a decent amount of retail experience under my belt, so when I applied for a job, Venus Envy hired me.

My job was to sell sex toys, provide sex education to customers and give workshops across the province, at private events, bachelorette parties and even senior’s facilities. I talked to people about everything from consent to blowjobs. At first, I felt like an imposter. Right after I was hired, I began reading every book about sex I could get my hands on. Eventually, I was a walking encyclopedia of sex knowledge, but I still had no clue what good sex actually felt like.

One day, about six months after I started, a customer asked if the vibrator I was recommending had worked for me. I felt caught, and after mumbling a very unconvincing lie, I decided to take matters into my own hands. I started practising all the things I’d been reading about, first on my own, then with partners. I quickly discovered that the people having the best sex were the ones who’d thrown out the idea that it had to look any certain way. They weren’t making assumptions that all guys like to dominate or that all women want to be submissive. Sex could be experimental, playful and freeing. At Venus Envy, I met other disabled people with flourishing sex lives. Suddenly, it clicked for me—I didn’t need to be able bodied or look a certain way to be hot.

In fact, my disability helped me become a great sex educator. People often worry about saying the wrong thing around me, so I have tons of experience making them feel comfortable with my body. It felt like an easy transition to helping people feel more at home in their own bodies. I instinctively knew how to listen to people’s fears and insecurities, free of judgment. I loved my job, even with all its uncomfortable quirks. Once, I gave a safe-sex presentation to thousands of first-year students at Dalhousie. It involved putting a condom on a dildo and demonstrating how to give a blowjob. For some people, a gig like that would be a nightmare. I lived for it.

I quickly realized, though, that all of the books and resources I was turning to for guidance had been written for people who are able bodied. So I started a blog, The Fucking Facts, to document the pleasure and joy of sex for people with disabilities. About a year into it, I was at a party, and one of my friends introduced me to Robbie MacGregor, who ran Invisible Publishing. My friend said that I should write a book for him, and he casually agreed. He sent me a very kind email the next day, encouraging me to go through with it. I was thrilled and immediately signed on.

The result of that conversation was _Hot, Wet and Shaking_, a memoir and essay collection about the lessons I learned in my early twenties. At its core, it’s a book about what it means to fall in love with your body, particularly as someone with a disability. It’s also about learning how to have good sex and lots of it. When it came out, I was on the cover of the local paper, and I got to tour the book across the country. Even though its content is very revealing and personal, I had no regrets.

I continued working at Venus Envy until my early thirties. In 2017, I moved to Toronto. I was commuting to Guelph to get my masters of science in couples and family therapy. While there, I specialized in healing from sexual trauma. Although I still believe sex is empowering, I know it can also be complicated. In a lot of ways, the work is very similar to what I’d been doing for years—helping others process shame, fear and failed expectations. After I finished my degree, I was hired at a couples therapy clinic in Toronto, and I eventually left to open up my own private practice.

[_**Related:** “My postpartum burnout nearly broke me. Now, I’ve opened a postnatal retreat for new parents”_](https://torontolife.com/city/melissa-gallagher-postpartum-burnout-anxiety-alma-care/)

Then, in October of 2022, I was shocked to receive a diagnosis of rapidly growing cancer in my bladder. They immediately planned for an emergency surgery, so quickly that my CT scans hadn’t even been processed yet. The scans didn’t come through until the day before the surgery, and when my doctor called me, it was with even more bad news: it was too late, he said. They could now see that my cancer was terminal. He told me to go eat my favourite foods. It felt like I was being served my last meal. Passing the news on to my friends and family was incredibly hard. Many people came over that day, bringing breakfast, coffee and whiskey. We spent the whole day eating, drinking and crying together.

Whether I wanted to or not, cancer forced me to take a step back and re-examine how I’d lived my life. I’ve always been an energetic person, and so much of my career and personal life has revolved around helping other people—as a sex educator, a sex partner, a therapist. I’ve always been a workaholic, and I rarely slowed down to consider my own needs. With cancer, my body physically can’t keep up with that lifestyle. I had to take a year off work after the diagnosis. My energy was simply too low. These days, I work part time, and I spend many of my other hours reading, lying down or swimming.

This year, I got a call from my publisher about a ten-year anniversary re-publication of _Hot, Wet and Shaking_. I’m so much more reluctant to share the intimate details of my sex life these days. While I still manage to have a fulfilling one, it’s more challenging now. Sometimes I have to cancel dates because I’m simply too tired. I’ve always been a magnet for pleasure, and having to seriously consider my physical limitations doesn’t come naturally to me. If _Hot, Wet and Shaking_ was about experiencing my body as a vessel for pleasure, the years since my diagnosis have been about learning how to accept that my body can also experience great pain. And even though I find my 25-year-old self cringey and embarrassing, I don’t regret that book. It was a much-needed celebration of sex, and besides, we’re all cringey and embarrassing sometimes—I know I still am. So I thought, _Why the hell not?_

Facing death has been a devastating process, but I’m trying to reframe my circumstances. I still experience so much joy, whether through sex or through spending time with friends and family. Back when I wrote my book, it felt revolutionary for me to be so publicly adoring of myself. In a society where disabled bodies are often seen as objects of pity, I still think it’s important work. But, ten years and one cancer diagnosis later, I’ve learned that life is full of both joy and profound suffering. It’s easy to rejoice publicly, but it’s a lot harder to express sadness. I have found, though, that when I’m honest about how hard it can feel to be alive, disabled and facing death, I feel less alone. People join me in my grief—they admit that they’re sad too. It’s within this shared space of love and celebration and grief that I feel the most healed.

![Image 1](https://www.geeksout.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/michele-kirichanskaya_avatar-96x96.jpg)

By: Michele Kirichanskaya

[Kaleigh Trace](https://invisiblepublishing.com/authors/kaleigh-trace/) is a writer and therapist living in Toronto. In a previous life she made sex education her business. Her first book, _Hot, Wet, and Shaking: How I Learned to Talk about Sex_ was published in 2014 and won the Evelyn Richardson Non-Fiction Award. In 2024, Invisible published a 10th anniversary edition with additional essays and a foreword from Christa Couture. Kaleigh’s work has also appeared in _Toronto Star_, _Toronto Life_, _The Coast_, _Shameless Magazine_, and on CBC Radio’s “Tapestry”. Kaleigh has a Masters of Science in Couple’s and Family Therapy and passable punch-needling skills.

I had the opportunity to interview Kaleigh, which you can read below.

_CW: Discussion of sexual material_

**First of all, welcome to Geeks OUT! Could you tell us a little about yourself?**

I am a queer, disabled couples & sex therapist and a writer. I split my time between Toronto and Nova Scotia because I struggle with commitment. I love sharing a knowing look with a stranger when a cute dog walks by; I hate the feeling of a drip of water sliding down the length of my arm after I’ve washed my face.

**What can you tell us about your book,** **_Hot, Wet, and Shaking: How I Learned to Talk about Sex,_** **which will have its 10****th** **anniversary publication in June****? What was the original inspiration for this project?**

I am so excited that this project gets to have a second coming (there’s a sex pun in there somewhere).

When I wrote Hot, Wet & Shaking ten years ago I was a sex educator in my mid-20’s, excited about coming out, radicalized by having an abortion, eager to see representation of other disabled people in the world of sex writing. Now I’m in my mid-30’s and I’m older and more tired but still excited, radicalized and eager. Everything and nothing has changed and it feels excellent to visit with my younger self.

To add a twist – just a few weeks after my publishers invited me to republish a revised edition of this memoir, I was diagnosed with terminal cancer and given 2 years to live. So, I’ve been in an editorial conversation with my younger self throughout the process of planning for my death, and that has been wild and healing. Honestly, it has all felt like some kind of full circle ordained magic.

**_Hot, Wet, and Shaking: How I Learned to Talk about Sex_** **is said to be about** **sex, desire, and disability. Could you expand on this here?**

When I decided to write Hot, Wet & Shaking I had been working at a queer, feminist sex shop for five years. I would spend all day talking to people about their fantasies, their wants, their worries, their shame. Through these conversations I felt a real sense of communion, this feeling like “Oh, we’re all just animals, looking for a home” or however David Byrne put it. So, I wanted to write something that would expose us and unite us. Looking back, I had a hope that if I spoke openly and shamelessly about my own sexual desires, my foibles and fuck ups (of which there are plenty) then other people would also give up the bit and admit that they also wanted, erred, felt joy, felt shame. Ambitious! I don’t know that Hot, Wet & Shaking fully achieved this but I can say this: since publishing, readers have repeatedly told me their most embarrassing sexual secrets. If a friend shits their pants, I am the first one they call. I have stood in front of crowds, a visibly disabled woman, and been understood as an object of desire. So, I guess this is what the book is about – our relatable humanness, our collective mistakes, and the right to be audaciously horny.

**As a writer, what drew you to the art of writing?**

I know that I have had the true and genuine privilege of publishing a book, but I still feel shy calling myself a writer. Like, who me?! I’m imperfect and insecure and uneducated, genuinely, about the act of writing. But I return to it over and over because for me, writing is about being in conversation with myself. It centers me inside my own life, and after I have written out my thoughts, experiences and sensations I feel a sort of invincibility, that I’ll be ok no matter what, even through death. I think about death a lot these days, as mine approaches. The psychoanalyst Winnicott said “ Oh God! May I be alive when I die!”. Writing makes me feel like that – really fucking alive.

![Image 2](https://www.geeksout.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/HWS-Cover-96RGB.jpg)

**How would you describe your creative process?**

I’m an extrovert through and through, and a Sagitarrius rising, if you’re into that kind of thing. So I can only write if I am full up of human relationships. I like to write when I get home from a party, or after a long phone call with a friend. I like writing best in bars and cafés – I want to half listen to the conversation at the next table while I think through syntax and structure. Maximum stimuli as creative process!

**As a writer, who or what would you say are some of your greatest creative influences and/or sources of inspiration in general?**

All of my writing exists in the context of other disabled writers, activists and thinkers. I could not write if not for the work of Eli Clare, Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samarasinha, Mia Mingus, Alice Wong, Chloé Cooper Jones, Christa Couture, Audre Lorde, Judith Heumann and Rebekah Taussig, to name only some.

**Aside from your work, what are some things you would want others to know about you?**

Oh my god, I wrote an extremely personal memoir about my sex life when I was 27! It’s all in there, there is truly nothing else I want anyone to know about me, I swear!

**What’s a question you haven’t been asked yet but that you wish you were asked (as well as the answer to that question)?**

The question – what song do you hope they play at your funeral and why?

The answer – Dragonette’s “Hello” because it is an absolutely perfect song, no notes, nothing makes me happier.

**What advice might you have to give for aspiring authors?**

There are something like 4 “successful” writers in Canada, if we’re marking success by financial gain. So write because it is for you and because it feeds you (metaphorically, because it won’t feed you literally).

Oh, and build a good relationship with a strong editor.

**Finally, what books/authors would you recommend to the readers of Geeks OUT?**

I can’t stop reading the poetry of Hanif Abdurraqib, Ross Gay and Ada Limón. All so life giving!

* * *

_Header Photo Credit Zoe Davison_

[Tapestry](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/tapestry/rethinking-disability-1.4726131)

Kaleigh Trace loves her body, but this wasn’t always the case. It took time for Trace to redefine conceptions of beauty and desirability. She speaks with guest host Christa Couture about her journey back to self-love.

![Image 1](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.4158517,1497373218000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C77%2C1500%2C843%29%3B)

Sex educator Kaleigh Trace says there are a lot of misconceptions about disability and sexual desire.

Kaleigh Trace loves her body.

The Halifax-based sex educator and author of the book, _Hot Wet and Shaking: How I Learned to Talk About Sex,_ says she loves different parts of herself in different ways.

"It's easy to love having blonde hair and blue eyes," Trace told [Tapestry](http://www.cbc.ca/tapestry) guest host Christa Couture, "but I think I more actively love the parts of my body that aren't normative. I really love my feet even though they look so different."

But that wasn't always the case.

*   [Rethinking disability](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/tapestry/rethinking-disability-1.4726131)

Rediscovering self-love
-----------------------

Just before she turned nine, Trace injured her spine in a car accident. As she got older, she started to feel self-conscious about her disability.

"As a kid, I didn't have a real problem with my body looking different but in teenhood, I really didn't like it at all and was ashamed of my difference and really hated it," said Trace.

Nowadays, Trace says she's rediscovered that feeling of self-love.

"Reclaiming what it means to feel comfortable in my body and really loving parts of it that are different has felt both new — but also almost like a returning to something I was able to feel when I was more naive and perhaps less entrenched in ideas of what is beautiful and valuable."

​

*   [My cerebral palsy isn't a problem to be cured, says writer Eli Clare](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/tapestry/rethinking-disability-1.4726131/my-cerebral-palsy-isn-t-a-problem-to-be-cured-says-writer-eli-clare-1.4726305)

Sex, dating and disability
--------------------------

During her twenties, Trace worked in a sex shop, which helped her redefine conceptions of beauty, value and desirability.

"The experience of being in your twenties and watching all styles of humans come in and have all styles of sexual desires and partners — it was so revolutionary," said Trace. "It really taught me a lot about the wide swath of human desirability and value."

Since then, she has written and spoken widely about disability and sex positivity.

"The biggest misconception about disability and sex is that people who are disabled don't have sexual desires and probably don't have sexual partners either because they're not desirable," said Trace.

​

*   [Inclusive design benefits everyone, not just people with disabilities](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/tapestry/rethinking-disability-1.4726131/inclusive-design-benefits-everyone-not-just-people-with-disabilities-1.4726333)

The pendulum swing of acceptance
--------------------------------

Much of Trace's work is defined by her unflinching love of herself and her disability, but she shared that she still experiences moments where acceptance is difficult.

"I think as humans, we kind of pendulum swing, and when I wrote the book I had just pendulum swung to finally being totally in love with myself," said Trace.

"Less often than ever before — but I still have moments when I feel in pain and miserable and embarrassed and ashamed."

Now, the struggle is to accept these moments as they come.

"I think I use to try and shove them away, just be like, 'No! I'm empowered now!'" said Trace.

She stressed that empowerment isn't a one way street.

"I think that being honest let's me be honest in that moment \[of doubt\] — and then I'm being just as honest the next day when I feel a bit better and think, 'damn, I look so good.'"

_Click LISTEN to hear Christa and Kaleigh Trace discuss the optics of dating apps and disability._

I believe that our relationships can be sites of powerful healing.
------------------------------------------------------------------

As a therapist it is an honour to work alongside couples, families and individuals as their relationships - to one another, to others, to themselves - transform. It is through this transformation that we come to better understand ourselves and create new ways of being that are more compassionate, empathetic and generative.

Prior to becoming a therapist I spent a decade working in sexual health education. I wrote and facilitated conversations about sexuality with the intention of healing shame and creating spaces of inclusion. My work as a therapist continues in this vein, and I am dedicated to bringing a stance of non-judgmental openness to the therapy room.

I am a person with a physical disability, and as such I have spent my life thinking critically about systems of power and privilege. I believe that therapy is justice-doing work and I advocate for and resist alongside clients.

I hold a Masters of Science in Couple & Family Therapy from the University of Guelph and I am a Registered Psychotherapist with the College of Registered Psychotherapists of Ontario.

Author and sex educator visits Sackville.

Halifax-based writer and educator Kaleigh Trace revels in promoting discussion about gender and sex. Last weekend, Trace brought these discussions to the Sackville community along with her newest book, _Hot, Wet, and Shaking_.

The event was organized by the newly reformed Women’s and Gender Studies Society and was hosted by Thunder & Lightning. It was part of a series of readings performed by the author along her tour that included stops ranging from the University of King’s College in Halifax, to New York City, to the University of Guelph.

As the crowd was settling in and enjoying refreshments, chatting with friends, and ordering drinks at the bar, Katharyn Stevenson, the president of the Women’s and Gender Studies Society, introduced both the topic of discussion for the night and the author herself. Once Stevenson took the microphone, the din died down and she broke into a reading of a formative work on sex, gender, and beauty: _The Beauty Myth_ by Naomi Wolf.

Stevenson chose an excerpt from Wolf linking societal expectations of beauty with the way we think about sex.

“The reader understands that she will have to look like \[a model\] in order to feel like that,” she read.

Stevenson continued by relating a personal account of how the understanding of sexuality and romantic relationships can differ in specific situations. Stevenson drew her introduction to a close by saying, “It’s okay to have your own sex story.”

Then it was time for Trace to take up the microphone to deliver a reading that was at once serious, thought-provoking, and hysterical.

But before all of this could happen, Trace gave the audience a brief overview of her past experiences and discussed the themes of her book. Trace describes herself as disabled, queer, and a sex educator. Her book _Hot, Wet, and Shaking_, as described on the back cover, “discusses her sexual exploits, bodily negotiations and attempts at adulthood, sparing none of the details and assuming you are not polite company.”

Trace read excerpts from three chapters of _Hot, Wet, and Shaking_ including “A Bag of Dicks,” “Looking for Blood,” and “(Not) Moving Like a Dyke/(Always) Dressing Like a Femme.” In these short readings, Trace moved from talking about the embarrassment of accidentally pulling a dildo out of one’s purse to negotiating the grounds of pregnancy tests and abortions.

Finally, Trace discussed the topic of figuring out whether one feels most comfortable in a plaid shirt matched with boots, or a skirt matched with anything pink, and the relationship between appearance and sexuality.

Trace spoke about each topic with humour and, more importantly, with a frank honesty that is frequently left out of normative discourses on sex and sexuality. Each of the stories at once demystified the topic at hand as well as encouraged the audience to accept that these topics are ones that everyone should feel comfortable discussing.

One of the evening’s most important excerpts came from Trace’s reading of “(Not) Moving Like a Dyke/(Always) Dressing Like a Femme.” As the story of how Trace had navigated the complex tangle of appearance and sexuality unfolded, she read, “Maybe queer could look my way too.

This summed up the message of the evening: sex and sexuality doesn’t have to look or feel a certain way, but every alternative narrative of sex should be welcomed and encouraged.

You can help by [editing the page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/List_of_LGBTQ_writers "Special:EditPage/List of LGBTQ writers") to add missing items, with references to [reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources").

This **list of LGBTQ writers** includes writers who are [lesbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesbian "Lesbian"), [gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay "Gay"), [bisexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bisexual "Bisexual"), [transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender") or [queer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queer "Queer") or otherwise [non-heterosexual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-heterosexual "Non-heterosexual"), [non-heteroromantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-heteroromantic "Non-heteroromantic") or [non-cisgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-cisgender "Non-cisgender") who have written about [LGBTQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ "LGBTQ") themes, elements or about LGBTQ issues. Works of these authors are part of [LGBT literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_literature "LGBT literature").

As this list includes writers from antiquity until the present, it is clearly understood that the term "LGBTQ" may not ideally describe the identity of all authors, particularly for those who wrote before the nineteenth century. In some cases, it is more useful to consider such authors as persons who expressed attractions for persons of the same sex (for example, Sappho or Plato), and avoid the anachronistic use of contemporary labels. Inclusion in this list follows general scholarly and academic norms, specified in references, that attempt to establish a genealogy or history of LGBTQ literature written by LGBTQ people. November 30, 2014

[_Station Eleven_ by Emily St. John Mandel](https://picklemethis.com/2014/11/30/station-eleven-by-emily-st-john-mandel/)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[![Image 1: station-eleven](https://picklemethis.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/station-eleven-204x300.jpg)](https://picklemethis.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/station-eleven.jpg)Lately, I’ve been reading off the beaten track (with more to come—so exciting! Up next is a copy of [_The Children’s Bach_](https://edgeofevening.wordpress.com/2014/04/19/the-childrens-bach/) by Helen Garner, and over the holidays I intend to read all four of Marilynne Robinson’s novels. And it thrills me so to read like this), but I am glad I came back down to earth to read [_Station Eleven_](http://www.mcnallyrobinson.com/product;isbn,9781443434867;at,aid546d009c70249#.VHvjtb54Xdl) by Emily St. John Mandel, which came recommended by [Nathalie Foy](http://nathaliefoy.wordpress.com/) and was nominated for [a National Book Award](http://www.nationalbook.org/nba2014.html#.VHvkOL54Xdk). With the latter point in particular, it doesn’t need a review from me, but I want to take a moment write about how much I enjoyed reading it. About how it didn’t immediately seem like something I’d appreciate—The Travelling Symphony, a troupe of actors and musicians, makes its way across America in the years following an apocalyptic flu pandemic that had brought the of civilization as we know it. That kind of setting rarely draws me—I like my books in civilization, thank you very much. But Mandel has a savvy knack of mixing it up, for turning the page at just the point my readerly patience is waning, and taking me somewhere altogether new. The novel moves between (seemingly) our present day and the not-s0-distant future, between Toronto on the eve of the pandemic, Hollywood some years before, and an airport in the future in which relics of the past—mobile phones, credit cards, games consoles, and more—have been preserved in a “Museum of Civilization.” The night of the flu outbreak, an actor dies onstage while performing King Lear at Toronto’s Elgin Theatre, a child actress in the wings watching, an audience member jumping on stage to per for CPR. And it turns out that Arthur Leander’s last night is the last night of everything, although memory of that night lives on in the mind of a few survivors connected to the actor. The survivors are also linked by a mysterious comic book whose narrative seems eerily prescient, and it turns out that this book about the end of the world is actually about the best of the world—the Travelling Symphony’s motto (written on their caravans, stolen from _Star Trek_) is, “Because survival is not enough,” after all.

And it’s not a book without hope. “If there are again towns with streetlights, if there are symphonies and newspapers, then what else might this awakening world contain?” Which is a question any of us could be asking any time, _Station Eleven_ a reminder that wonders are ever unceasing—the spell of a good book most certainly among them.

*   [Purchase Station Eleven from McNally Robinson](http://www.mcnallyrobinson.com/product;isbn,9781443434867;at,aid546d009c70249#.VHvjtb54Xdl)
